title: [Top 15: Amazon] How a Tool Built for Programmers Became a $5 Billion Business
excerpt: Quietly, AWS has become Amazon's most promising business
body:
Quietly, AWS has become Amazon's most promising business

"This is a $5 billion business a year, and it's still accelerating." That is how Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos described AWS, the cloud computing business Amazon has run for more than a decade, late last month.

It was the first time Amazon had disclosed AWS (short for Amazon Web Services) revenue since the business began. Until then, no one could say how much it really mattered to an e-commerce company.

Unlike the books, Kindles and children's toys that Amazon sells on its website, AWS sells computing power. Amazon has built dozens of data centers around the world, filled with tens of thousands of computers. Its customers don't have to build their own server rooms. They simply pay to use those computers to run websites, store data and carry out all kinds of complex computations.

It works much like a power company: power stations generate electricity and send it through the grid to every business, and businesses pay for it instead of buying their own generators. The difference is that a power station can run for decades, while computer processors are upgraded far faster. A cloud computing service has to keep replacing its equipment and keep cutting its prices at the same time. Since 2006, AWS has cut prices 48 times.

So a question has hung over it: can a business that needs constant new investment, while its product keeps getting cheaper, actually make money?

It now seems it can. Over the past three months, AWS brought Amazon US$1.56 billion in revenue and US$265 million in profit. Set that beside the retail profits of Amazon's website and it is plain that AWS has become a major pillar of Amazon's earnings ([or rather, of stemming its losses](http://www.qdaily.com/display/cards/5866.html)):

![Chart comparing AWS profit with Amazon's retail profit](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021057308Y6q0uG17RFfklAT.jpg-w600)

Few people expected AWS to be this profitable. On the day the figures came out, Amazon's market value jumped US$25.6 billion, more than Google was worth when it went public. And this happened even as Amazon's e-commerce business posted another loss. [Some analysts argue](https://stratechery.com/2015/the-aws-ipo/) that the jump reflects what investors think AWS is really worth.

More than one million paying customers now use AWS every day. Philips uses it to [analyze 390 million medical records](https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/philips/), the hit mobile game Clash of Clans runs its online battles on it, and Stanford stores its open courses there. Even NASA's analysis of Mars photos and the CIA's intelligence analysis run on AWS. Its market share is larger than that of the next three players, Microsoft, IBM and Google, combined:

![Chart of cloud infrastructure market share: AWS versus Microsoft, IBM and Google](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702105731aF8KbZTtzVDOhHMu.jpg-w600)

*Data from Synergy Research Group*

AWS plainly does not sell to ordinary consumers the way books, potato chips or the Kindle do. And more than ten years ago, Microsoft, Google and IBM all had far more technical experience than Amazon.

So why was it Amazon that pulled this off?

## It started with a product catalog

We interviewed Jeff Barr, AWS's chief evangelist. Barr, whose job is to explain technical details to users, has worked at Amazon for 13 years and has been involved with AWS since the beginning.

In the second half of 2002, Barr was running his own consulting firm, advising young internet companies on technology. He had watched computing grow up: he started programming at 17 and by then had 25 years of software development behind him.

That year, Amazon launched a service called Amazon.com Web Services. Put simply, Amazon put information about its products, such as sales ranks, prices, names and publishers, into a database and opened it up through an interface (API).

Think of someone building a camera app today. They don't actually know how a phone's camera works, and they don't need to. The phone's operating system already handles taking pictures; the developer only has to hook the app up to a virtual interface to control the camera.

That saves developers from writing hundreds of lines of code to drive the camera, so they can spend the effort on more distinctive features, such as skin-smoothing or filters. In the same way, developers could look up product information directly through Amazon.com Web Services instead of picking apart the content of the whole website.

Someone used it, for example, to build a price-lookup service that looks rather primitive today: you texted the number printed on the back of a book to a designated phone number and got back the book's price on Amazon.

Amazon.com Web Services did little, but very few websites were trying anything like it at the time, so it still drew some users. Barr was one of the early ones and wrote two small programs with it. Later that year, he went to a developer conference Amazon held in Seattle.

The "conference" drew four or five developers, fewer than the Amazon staff in the room. But Bezos, already a business star, came in person to pitch his new idea. At the event, an Amazon engineer said the company would put more and richer functions online through interfaces.

"Before that, I had worked on a lot of projects around early internet services, always thinking that one day big companies would use these services too. When I saw Amazon trying to commercialize internet services, I felt this was the future I wanted," Barr recalled in an interview with QDaily. After the event he asked Amazon for an interview and joined the company.

## Solving Amazon's own problem

Opening up product information alone could not make a $5 billion business. The turning point came in 2003, with a major internal overhaul at Amazon.

Amazon was then eight years old and sold hundreds of millions of items a year. Behind the scenes, dozens of development teams worked on separate projects. But to keep things manageable, server resources were pooled and run by a single department, and every new project needed approval before it could get any.

According to the book *The Everything Store*, by 2003 this setup had broken down. Even some important projects could not be tested in advance because they could not secure enough servers.

The trouble was not only hardware. Getting software built separately by dozens of teams to work together also slowed the whole organization down.

Steve Yegge, an engineer who worked at Amazon and later joined Google, [recalled in an article](http://coolshell.cn/articles/5701.html%0A) years later that Bezos emailed the technical teams with an order: every project inside the company had to be built as a general-purpose function and exposed to other teams through an interface, much like a phone's camera. Teams would no longer need to go back and forth with one another. They could call the relevant interface to get the servers they needed, or another team's work, and so move their own projects faster. Bezos reportedly threatened in the email to fire anyone who did not comply.

"Developers are alchemists, and our job is to do everything we can to let them do their alchemy," Bezos once said, explaining the changes to the internal platform. It was a very unusual step, and the first time a large internet company had done anything like it.

Amazon was not the only company with alchemists, and Amazon's were not the only alchemists who needed a better place to work. Having solved its own problem, Amazon naturally began to consider turning AWS into such a platform and selling it to other companies as a paid service.

The new AWS team was put under Andy Jassy, an executive Bezos valued highly. In late 2003, Jassy wrote the plan for the project, and Barr helped revise it.

## Serving programmers, not CEOs

A joke about Hewlett-Packard has made the rounds for years: salespeople from IBM and HP go to call on a client. In the elevator, the IBM salesperson presses the top floor, to see the CEO. The HP salesperson presses the basement, because that's where the IT department is.

When Amazon began promoting AWS as an IT service, it did not go to the top floor to find the CEO. In fact, it did not go after companies big enough to fill a building at all.

"At the beginning, the whole team was Andy, me, and five developers," Barr told QDaily. There was no sales staff and no advertising, and he alone handled outreach. His target was clear: programmers who liked to tinker with new tools on their own.

From 2003 on, Barr turned up wherever programmers gathered, from technical seminars to the early meetups where people kicked around the idea of cloud computing.

"Basically, wherever there were developers, we were there," Barr recalled. "In the very early days, I sometimes had to explain to people what amazon.com did."

Besides conferences, Barr promoted AWS through blogs, which programmers love. In November 2004, the official AWS blog went live. In a post of fewer than 100 words, Barr announced the blog and said AWS's developer relations team would share all kinds of AWS news there. You can [still read that post on Amazon today](https://aws.amazon.com/cn/blogs/aws/welcome/).

Between writing technical documentation and going out to explain the idea of online services, Barr wrote a short post every two or three days on the new features AWS had launched, technical documents to help with development, and new tools developers had built with it.

By 2006, when AWS's two heavyweight products, the S3 cloud storage service and EC2, launched one after the other, Barr and a team of a few people had spent more than two years promoting AWS and the idea of cloud computing among developers. Within days of EC2's launch, every computer Amazon had set aside for it in its data centers was taken.

You can think of S3 as a hard drive that can grow without limit. EC2 is a virtual platform on which a developer can bring a computer, operating system already installed, online and working within minutes.

For the next several years, most of Amazon's marketing was aimed squarely at programmers. Adam FitzGerald, Amazon's head of global developer marketing, told QDaily: "Programmers are interested in solving technical problems, not in fancy marketing language. If you can help them solve problems, what's more useful to them is a sense of community built around the tools."

Technical people like to share how they solved a problem with a tool, not how they got a big company to solve it for them. Because AWS was pitched as a tool, the very users it targeted became its most eager promoters. Adrian Cockcroft, Netflix's head of cloud computing, was one of AWS's biggest champions. For four or five years, at every technical event he attended, he talked about how Netflix used AWS to meet its enormous demand.

Even AWS's first appearance on the heavily trafficked *New York Times* website came not from advertising or a press conference, but from the paper's own engineers, who published an article on how they used AWS to scan every *Times* news story from the 19th century into digital images and store them on AWS. Had IBM been the one solving the *Times*'s technical problem, it is hard to imagine we would have read such a story.

This positioning helped Amazon catch a new wave.

## Growing with startups

In 2006, just as AWS was releasing one heavyweight product after another, the shadow of the first internet bubble was lifting and a new generation of internet startups began to appear in large numbers. Soon after, with the arrival of the iPhone and Android smartphones, mobile apps became the new startup trend.

Popular startups such as Airbnb and Instagram were founded in this period. Companies that had been around for a while, such as Netflix and Rovio, also found new growth in these years.

All of these companies were AWS customers, because the way AWS was sold suited small teams almost perfectly.

Although it was built to solve companies' IT problems, AWS was more a tool sold to programmers than an enterprise service sold to CEOs. Users never had to deal with a salesperson. They signed in on a web page with their Amazon account and started using AWS, and payment was charged automatically to the credit card linked to that account. This way of selling was a near-perfect fit for small teams that lacked the people and the money to fuss with enterprise services.

AWS also overturned the traditional IT sales model. It broke computing resources into small measurable units such as CPU hours, gigabytes of disk storage and bandwidth, so developers no longer paid by the piece of hardware. Startups could rent more as they grew, instead of paying a large sum up front. If a startup failed, it only had to stop the service, with no servers left over to get rid of.

Over the following years, many startups' use of AWS grew quickly along with their businesses. Netflix, which began pushing its monthly online video subscription in 2008, ran all the computing for storing and streaming its films on AWS. By 2014, Netflix had grown from an unremarkable disc-rental site into an online video giant that accounted for 34% of all downstream internet traffic in the United States at peak hours.

Microsoft and Google also wanted to sell cloud computing to companies of every size. But as two established tech giants, they at first asked startups to adopt their own technical standards, such as Microsoft's programming languages and databases, and in the very beginning even the Windows operating system. Startups building from scratch were not willing to accept such limits.

In 2011, someone counted the technologies used by 250 startups from Y Combinator, Silicon Valley's top startup incubator. Amazon came out on top: 87 of the companies hosted their services on AWS. Only nine used Google's services. For Microsoft, the number was zero.

## The market today

As the startups grew, so did AWS. Today it offers 40 services along the lines of EC2 and launches hundreds of new features a year. Since 2011, Amazon has been [hiring more than a hundred enterprise salespeople a year](http://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-enterprise-hires-2013-3), bringing traditional big companies such as Philips and Novartis onto AWS.

Its competitors woke up to the threat at about the same time, in 2011. Early that year, Steve Ballmer fired the executive then running Microsoft's cloud and enterprise business. His successor, Satya Nadella, made Azure, the cloud business that competes head-on with AWS, more and more open, including support for rivals' technologies, even though that meant eating into Microsoft's lucrative sales of Windows Server software and databases.

After Nadella succeeded Ballmer as Microsoft CEO in 2014, Scott Guthrie, head of the Azure engineering team and an avid writer of posts introducing new features on his technical blog, was promoted two levels to run the entire cloud and enterprise business. It is Microsoft's second-largest business, bigger than Windows, which shows how seriously Microsoft takes Azure.

Google and IBM, slower to react, began offering services similar to AWS in 2013, Google by building its own and IBM by acquisition. That same year, the CIA gave a US$600 million contract to Amazon rather than to IBM, which had far more experience working with the government.

AWS remains far ahead. By Deutsche Bank's estimate, Microsoft's Azure, its closest competitor, may be as little as one-tenth the size of AWS. But the gap is closing: Azure's sales grew by more than 100% in every quarter of the past year.

If competitors had any lingering doubt about the business of selling basic cloud computing, the figures Amazon just disclosed have settled it. Amazon has the advantages of moving first and of scale; Microsoft and Google have deeper pockets.

Amazon began by giving programmers a better workbench, and it ended up upending the enterprise IT market. Now a new round of competition begins.

## About the Top 15

In every era, a handful of companies attract the most capital and the best talent and shape how society develops. QDaily believes that the companies shaping the way we live are the core of today's business world.

So we have chosen the 15 most important lifestyle companies in the world and in China: [Apple](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/8963.html), [Google](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/7936.html), Baidu, [Alibaba](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/9234.html), Tencent, Amazon, Disney, [McDonald's](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/9029.html), Starbucks, Nike, Xiaomi, IKEA, Uniqlo, Wanda and Vanke. The list will change as the companies' businesses, markets and trends change. We will follow them, and their competitors and partners too.

Over the next month, we will publish a series of reports on how these companies are doing.
